newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AUSTRALIA TRANSPORT - General freight rates seen rising.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AUSTRALIA TRANSPORT - General freight rates seen rising.

text.p: Australian general freight rates are likely to rise following the exit of most of Australia's major transport companies from this sector in the past two years, a transport industry expert said.

"I would speculate that the pressure which caused the large companies to divest themselves of general freight, which is to say low rates, must be turned around," Tim Peken, a partner of law firm Deacons Graham and James, told Reuters in an interview.

Peken, who specialises in road transport law and has 30 years transport sector experience, said medium sized transport firms were likely to suffer the same price pressure which caused larger companies to exit general freight.

"I think that rates are going to have to increase - unless there is a significant increase in the rates, then those companies that have filled the void left by the majors will suffer the same economic pressures and will be forced to pull out as well," he said.
In July, TNT Ltd, Australia's largest general freight operator, announced it was selling its general freight business.
TNT, which is now a unit of Dutch telecoms and postal group Koninklijke PTT Nederland, will be the last of the three biggest listed transport companies to get out of this difficult segment.

Earlier this year, Brambles Industries Ltd sold its four general freight businesses to Toll Holdings Ltd for A$25 million. Last year, Mayne Nickless Ltd sold its general freight operation, Interlink, to Toll for about A$15 million.
"It (the exit) is a result of the depressed rates that are available for general freight, that in turn is a result of the high level of competition," Peken said.
In the short term Peken expected the general freight market to become more competitive.

"One of the things that keeps the competition there is there is a lot of smaller companies that want to get bigger so there is always someone that is ready and willing to do the work - there are even people that are prepared to start up companies almost from scratch," he said.
The ease of entry into the general freight business in Australia meant there were a large number of independent truck owners that are willing to work for very low margins.
"There have always been a large number of lorry owner-drivers around - they have always been part of the background of the industry," Peken said.
The role Peken saw owner-drivers playing now was no different to before the major players exited.

"You're still not finding, and don't think will ever find, the very small operators being contractors direct to consignors. They will continue to be almost exclusively sub-contractors to large contractors," he said.

Pecken said small to medium sized transport companies had taken up the slack created by the exit of the major companies while the larger companies were continuing with specialised areas like armoured cars, time critical freight, car carriers, logistics, waste disposal, fuel and extra-heavy large loads.
"These are all areas that are still reasonably profitable partly because there are far greater barriers to entry to those specialised areas then there are to general freight," he said.
Pecken said the number of potential customers for these areas was much higher and by comparison the margins were also a lot higher.
